candidate_relations.reason: Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome is an autosomal dominant hereditary hamartomatous polyposis caused by STK11 mutations, characterized by mucocutaneous melanin deposits (perioral, buccal mucosa), and hamartomatous polyps. While the mucocutaneous pigmentation superficially overlaps, Cronkhite-Canada syndrome is a non-hereditary, non-familial acquired condition distinguished by its ectodermal triad (onychodystrophy, alopecia, skin hyperpigmentation on trunk/extremities), protein-losing enteropathy with severe hypoproteinemia/hypoalbuminemia, zinc and B12 deficiency, and inflammatory/cystic polyps (Yamada type II/III) rather than hamartomas. The patient's onychodystrophy, diffuse hyperpigmentation on trunk and extremities (not perioral/mucosal), severe nutritional deficiencies, and atrophic gastric mucosa with nodular lymphoid duodenal lesions are hallmarks of Cronkhite-Canada, not Peutz-Jeghers. Additionally, PJS typically presents with episodic obstruction/intussusception rather than secretory diarrhea of this magnitude.
candidate_relations.scope_detail: Different hamartomatous polyposis syndrome with incompatible etiology and clinical profile

case_quality_flags: Patient age (15 years) is atypically young for Cronkhite-Canada syndrome, which classically affects adults over 50; however, the full clinical constellation (ectodermal triad, protein-losing enteropathy, polyp morphology, nutritional deficiencies) strongly supports this diagnosis over alternatives
Alopecia not explicitly mentioned in the record, though onychodystrophy and skin findings satisfy partial ectodermal triad criteria
